summary: toString() sets the text an object shows in a template literal or String(). JavaScript has no equals hook, so you write an equals() method and call it yourself.
notes: console.log(a) prints the fields, Student { name: 'Maya', studentId: 1001 }. Use String(a) or a template literal to get toString().
=== and includes() both compare objects by identity, so roster.includes(b) is false.
roster.some((s) => s.equals(b)) checks each item with your own equals() method.
pitfall: Comparing two students with === or == gives false even when their data matches, because both check whether they are the same object. Call a.equals(b) instead.
contrast: Python's == and Java's contains() both call your equality method, but JavaScript's === and includes() always check identity. JavaScript uses toString() in template literals, but console.log(object) shows the fields instead.
